subsection: 6. The Catholic Church, the GAA, Protestant churches and the Orange Order abroad

notes.h: Why church and club mattered to emigrants
notes.b: Mass emigration after 1840, above all during the Famine, sent huge numbers of poor Irish Catholics to the USA, Britain, Canada and Australia. Church and club gave them shelter and community in countries where many people looked down on them.
points: Most Irish Catholic emigrants after 1840 were poor, so they arrived with little money, which made shared institutions such as the parish very valuable.
Emigrants often met prejudice as poor Catholics (discrimination means unequal treatment because of religion or origin), so the church and later the GAA gave them a place where they were welcome.
Two outcomes are set against each other: assimilation (emigrants and their children adopting the culture of the new country) and preservation of Irish identity.

The Protestant side is different. Ulster Protestants (Presbyterians, Anglicans and Methodists, loyal to the Crown) had been emigrating long before the Famine, so their story starts earlier and has a different shape.

Irish priests and nuns also went abroad as missionaries beyond the emigrant communities, a link sometimes called Ireland's spiritual empire, but here the focus is on churches serving emigrants themselves.
notes.tip: In essays, open with a judgement on how far these institutions sustained Irishness, and remember that assimilation of the children is the main counter-argument.

notes.h: The Catholic Church in the United States: hierarchy and parishes
notes.b: Irish priests and bishops led the Catholic Church in America, and its parishes became the centre of Irish emigrant life. This leadership kept a sense of Irishness alive in an English-speaking country.
points: Irish-born and Irish-American priests and bishops dominated the American Catholic hierarchy (the ranked leadership of bishops) for much of the 19th and early 20th centuries, because Irish emigrants were the largest Catholic group and spoke English.
John Hughes, born in Co. Tyrone in 1797, became archbishop of New York in 1850, which shows how quickly an Irish emigrant could rise to lead the American church.
John McCloskey, born in New York of Irish parents, became the first American cardinal (a senior church leader who helps choose the pope) in 1875.

Irish communities built parish churches (the local church serving one district), and many were dedicated to Irish saints such as Patrick and Brigid, so the buildings themselves announced an Irish identity.
St Patrick's Cathedral in New York was begun in 1858 and dedicated in 1879, and it became a symbol of the Irish-led Catholic presence in the city.
The parish was a social centre as well as a place of worship, with dances, sodalities (parish groups for prayer and fellowship) and sport, and the priest acted as adviser and community leader.
notes.tip: A one-sentence answer to who dominated the American hierarchy is the Irish, because they were the largest English-speaking Catholic group. Do not mix up John Hughes the archbishop with Billy Hughes the Australian prime minister.

notes.h: The Catholic Church in the United States: schools, orders and societies
notes.b: Beyond the parish itself, the church built schools, hospitals and societies that looked after emigrants from childhood to burial. Many were run by Irish-born or Irish-descended members.
points: The Third Plenary Council of Baltimore in 1884 (a national meeting of American bishops) required every parish to have a school within two years, which made parochial schools central to Catholic life.

Religious orders with Irish members, including the Sisters of Mercy (founded in Dublin by Catherine McAuley in 1831) and the Christian Brothers, ran schools, hospitals and charitable houses in the USA, Britain and Australia.
Catholic fraternal societies (clubs whose members pay in and help one another) offered insurance, funeral benefits and social life, which mattered because poor emigrants had no other safety net.
The Ancient Order of Hibernians, a Catholic Irish fraternal society, was founded in New York in 1836.

The Knights of Columbus was founded in 1882 in New Haven, Connecticut, by Michael McGivney, a priest and son of Irish immigrants. It was a Catholic society with a mixed membership, not an exclusively Irish one.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level answers on the Church usually need Baltimore 1884 and parish schools, societies, and orders running schools and hospitals. Do not call the Knights of Columbus an Irish society.

notes.h: The Catholic Church in Britain and Australia
notes.b: In Britain and Australia the Irish were again the backbone of the Catholic Church, and its institutions served poor congregations that the state did little for. In both countries the church was a visible minority, so it attracted both loyalty and suspicion.
points: Irish-born priests served many Catholic parishes in Liverpool, Glasgow and other British cities, where they built churches and schools for poor congregations.
The Catholic hierarchy was restored in England and Wales in 1850 (bishops with their own districts again), at a time when Famine emigration was swelling Catholic numbers.
The Education (Scotland) Act of 1918 brought Catholic schools in Scotland into the state system while keeping their religious character, which secured their place in Scottish education.

Brother Walfrid (born Andrew Kerins in Ballymote, Co. Sligo), a Marist Brother, founded Celtic F.C. in Glasgow in 1887 to raise money for poor Catholic families in the East End. The club became a symbol of the Irish community in Scotland.
Irish nuns ran hospitals, orphanages and schools in British cities, and their work reached poor Irish districts that the state had not served well.
In Australia the church was led largely by Irish-born clergy and bishops, and Irish orders such as the Christian Brothers and the Sisters of Mercy staffed its schools.

Colonies ended state aid to church schools in the 1870s and 1880s, for example Victoria in 1872 and New South Wales in 1880. The Catholic Church then built its own school system, staffed by Irish orders and funded by the Irish Catholic community.

Because Catholics were a visible minority in Britain and Australia, their institutions were a focus both for loyalty to the Irish cause and for sectarian suspicion (hostility between religious groups).
notes.tip: Brother Walfrid and Celtic F.C. belong to the Church in Britain, not to the GAA: Celtic was a football club. Learn the dates 1850, 1887 and 1918 separately.

notes.h: The Catholic Church and the Irish in Canada
notes.b: Irish Catholics were the largest Catholic group in English-speaking Canada, so the church there grew around their needs. In Ontario it came into steady conflict with the Orange Order.
points: The church built parishes, schools and hospitals in Montreal, Toronto and Ontario towns for the growing Irish Catholic population.
St Patrick's Basilica in Montreal opened in 1847 to serve the city's growing Irish Catholic congregation.

Michael Power, the first Catholic bishop of Toronto, was born in Nova Scotia to Irish parents. He died of typhus in October 1847 after caring for Famine emigrants, which shows the church sharing the dangers the emigrants faced.
In Newfoundland people of Irish Catholic descent formed a large share of the population, so the church was central to their community life.
In Ontario Catholic and Orange rivalry was constant, and disputes over separate Catholic schools (schools funded and run apart from the main public system) were a recurring political issue.
notes.tip: In answers on Canada, give the church's parishes, schools and hospitals, and note the constant Catholic and Orange rivalry in Ontario, including the dispute over separate Catholic schools.

notes.b: Daniel Mannix was an Irish-born Catholic archbishop in Melbourne. His opposition to conscription and his support for Irish independence made him a controversial figure, admired by some and attacked by others.
points: Daniel Mannix was born in Charleville, Co. Cork, in 1864, trained as a priest at Maynooth and was president of Maynooth College from 1903 until 1912.
He was appointed coadjutor archbishop of Melbourne in 1912, an assistant bishop with the right to succeed, and he became archbishop in 1917. He died in November 1963, aged 99.

He opposed conscription (compulsory military service) in the referendums of October 1916 and December 1917, both of which were defeated. He was most prominent in the 1917 campaign, and it brought him into conflict with Prime Minister Billy Hughes and imperial loyalists, who called him disloyal.
He supported Irish independence and criticised British policy in Ireland after 1916.

In August 1920, on a voyage from the USA towards Ireland, a British naval vessel took him off his ship and landed him in England. He was banned from Ireland and some British cities with large Irish populations, but went on to speak to Irish Catholics in Britain.

He clashed with the Orange Order and other Protestant organisations in Victoria, and sectarian disputes shaped Melbourne politics in his time. His stand grew out of Irish-Australian Catholic grievance and the pressures of the First World War, so he was shaped by events as well as shaping them.
In the 1950s he supported the anti-communist Catholic Movement led by B. A. Santamaria, which contributed to the Australian Labor Party split of 1955.
Contemporary attitudes were sharply divided. Irish Australians and many Catholics admired him, while imperial loyalists and Protestant organisations in Australia denounced him as disloyal.
Historians present him as a major figure in Australian Catholic and political life, and they debate how far his nationalism was an Irish-Australian response to anti-Catholic prejudice.
notes.tip: Each correct dated point earns credit, so learn Charleville 1864, Maynooth president 1903-12, coadjutor 1912 and archbishop 1917. State that he opposed conscription in both referendums but was most prominent in 1917, and finish with one assessment point.

notes.b: The Gaelic Athletic Association was founded in Ireland in 1884 to promote Irish sport, and it followed emigrants overseas through clubs and tours. It tied sport to nationalism, so its clubs abroad were part of the same Irish culture.
points: The GAA was founded at Hayes's Hotel in Thurles, Co. Tipperary, on 1 November 1884, and its founders included Michael Cusack and Maurice Davin.
It promoted Gaelic football and hurling and also organised athletics, as a way of building a distinctly Irish sporting culture.

The GAA linked sport with nationalism by banning members from playing or attending foreign games, a rule that tied the association to nationalism. Clubs abroad belonged to the same nationalist culture.

In 1888 a party of Irish athletes, hurlers and footballers toured the United States, playing exhibition matches and athletics before Irish-American crowds. The tour lost money, and some of the party stayed in America.
Clubs playing Gaelic football and hurling appeared in New York, Chicago, Boston and other cities with large Irish populations, and New York became the main centre in North America.
A London GAA board was established in the 1890s, and clubs in Britain and Australia gave emigrants a regular social life built around their identity.
The 1947 All-Ireland football final between Cavan and Kerry, which Cavan won, was played at the Polo Grounds in New York, to mark the Irish diaspora's place in the association.
notes.tip: Learn the GAA founding as place, date and founders, plus its purpose, clubs abroad and the 1888 tour (lost money, some stayed). Do not date the ban on foreign games, and do not confuse the 1884 founding with the 1888 tour.

notes.b: Protestant emigrants from Ulster kept a Presbyterian and Methodist identity that was distinct from Irish Catholic nationalism. It rested on descent, religion and loyalty to the Crown, not on parish and school as for Catholics.
points: Ulster Presbyterians settled in Pennsylvania and along the Appalachians in the 18th century. Francis Makemie, born near Ramelton, Co. Donegal, was a leading figure in founding American Presbyterianism, with the first presbytery (a governing council of ministers) in Philadelphia in 1706.

Their descendants in the USA became known as Scotch-Irish. The term was in use earlier but became more common from the 19th century, especially after the Famine, to distinguish Protestants from Catholic Irish.
Presbyterian and Methodist congregations in the USA and Canada kept links with the churches in Ireland and recruited ministers from them.
Philip Embury and Barbara Heck, Palatines (Protestants of German origin) from Co. Limerick, helped found the first Methodist society in New York in the 1760s.
The Ulster-Scots identity stressed Protestant descent, loyalty to the British Crown and a heritage separate from the Irish Catholic majority.
Many Protestant emigrants assimilated quickly into American and Canadian denominations, so their sense of Irishness faded faster than that of Catholics.
In Canada Ulster-Scots and Presbyterian identity was strong in Ontario, and it was tied to loyalty to the British connection.
notes.tip: Strong answers contrast Catholic identity, which was institutional (parish, school, society) and lasted, with Ulster-Scots identity, which rested on descent, Presbyterianism and loyalty to the Crown and faded faster. Define the Scotch-Irish in one sentence.

notes.h: The Orange Order in Canada and Australia
notes.b: The Orange Order, a Protestant and loyalist society, was founded in Ireland in 1795 and carried its identity to Canada and Australia, where it became politically significant. Where it met Catholic institutions, the old sectarian rivalry was renewed.
points: The Orange Order was founded in Co. Armagh in 1795, after the Battle of the Diamond between Protestant and Catholic groups in September of that year.

Lodges (the local units of the Order) reached Canada early in the 19th century with soldiers and settlers. The Grand Orange Lodge of British America was formed in 1830, in Ontario, to coordinate them.
Toronto, called the Belfast of Canada, had many Orange mayors. This shows the Order's political power in Toronto and Ontario.
Sir John A. Macdonald, Canada's first prime minister, was an Orangeman, and Mackenzie Bowell, prime minister from December 1894 to April 1896, was a Grand Master.
Orange parades on 12 July, known as the Twelfth, marked the Battle of the Boyne of 1690 and were occasions of public display and occasional violence in Canada.
Orange lodges were established in colonial New South Wales from the 1840s and later in Victoria, where they opposed Catholic influence and Home Rule (self-government for Ireland).
In Australia the Order was part of a loyalist and anti-Catholic culture, and it clashed with Catholic institutions in Melbourne and Sydney.

Orange parades in New York in July 1870 and July 1871 led to riots with Irish Catholics in which dozens died in total, far more in 1871 than in 1870. This shows that Irish sectarian rivalry was carried to America.
notes.tip: Orange Order answers reward the Canadian political power (Toronto mayors, Macdonald, Bowell) and the Twelfth. An answer that describes only Canada loses marks on Australia, where you need the opposition to Catholic influence and Home Rule.

notes.h: How church, sport and community sustained Irishness
notes.b: Church, sport and community life worked together to sustain a sense of Irishness abroad, though many emigrants and their children took part in only some of them. They also pushed emigrants toward their new countries.
points: Priests and nuns acted as community leaders, and parish events such as dances, picnics and fundraising kept Irish life visible in the city.
St Patrick's Day parades in New York date back to 1762, when Irish soldiers serving in the British army first held one. They became a major public display of Irish identity in America.
Church schools taught Catholic children their faith and gave the second generation a grounding in parish and community life.
The second generation often moved towards American or Australian culture, so the church and GAA supported Irishness mainly for those who wanted it.
Catholic and Orange rivalry in Canada and Australia shaped the public life of Irish communities, so sectarian tension was a constant feature of emigrant life.
The Catholic Church encouraged loyalty to the new country as well as faith, so it was a vehicle of assimilation as well as of Irishness.
notes.tip: Argue both sides: the church preserved identity, but it also taught loyalty to the new country. That two-sided point is what a stated judgement needs.

notes.h: Assessment: church, sport and identity abroad
notes.b: Judging how far these institutions sustained Irishness means weighing what they achieved against who they missed. Contemporaries and later historians also disagreed about their effects.
points: Achievement: the Catholic Church and the GAA gave Irish emigrants a community, a social life and an Irish identity that lasted for generations. The church was the stronger of the two because it reached nearly every Catholic, while the GAA was narrower, more male and sporting.
Limit: many emigrants' children assimilated, so their Irishness weakened, and the institutions reached only part of the emigrant population.
Contemporary view: Irish nationalists praised the church and the GAA as guardians of Irishness, while nativists and imperial loyalists regarded them as divisive.
Later view: historians argue that the church and the GAA preserved identity but also helped Irish communities to organise and gain power in their new societies.
Protestant and Orange identity achieved political influence in Canada and Australia, but it expressed loyalty to the British connection, not Irish nationalism.
Sectarian rivalry was exported with the emigrants: Catholic against Orange in Canada, Australia, Britain and the USA.
notes.tip: The 100-mark essay usually asks how far the Church and the GAA sustained Irishness. State your judgement in the first lines, give both achievement and limit, and compare Church with GAA.

The sense of Ulster Presbyterian descent among emigrants in North America, often called Scotch-Irish, which stressed Protestant heritage and loyalty to the Crown.
The network of parish schools that the Catholic Church required in the USA from the 1884 Council of Baltimore.
A Catholic fraternal society for Irish men, offering insurance and social support to members abroad.
The term used in North America for descendants of Ulster Presbyterian settlers, who kept an identity separate from Irish Catholics.
The bishops and archbishops who govern a church; Irish-born and Irish-American clergy dominated the American Catholic hierarchy.
Hostility between religious groups, such as Catholics and Orangemen, which Irish emigrants carried into Canada, Australia, the USA and Britain.
The Orange parades held on 12 July to mark the Battle of the Boyne.
